stem: Which statement best describes **respiration**?

options.content: Breathing air in and out of the lungs
options.rationale: That is ventilation (breathing).

options.content: The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy
options.rationale: Respiration happens in every living cell.

options.content: The exchange of gases in the alveoli
options.rationale: That is gas exchange.

options.content: The making of glucose using light energy
options.rationale: That is photosynthesis.

explanation: Respiration is a set of chemical reactions, controlled by enzymes, that take place in all living cells and release energy from nutrient molecules such as glucose.
hints: It happens inside cells, not in the lungs.

stem: What are the products of aerobic respiration?

options.content: Glucose and oxygen
options.rationale: These are the reactants.

options.content: Lactic acid only
options.rationale: Lactic acid is made in anaerobic respiration in muscles.

options.content: Alcohol and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: These are made in anaerobic respiration in yeast.

options.content: Carbon dioxide and water
options.rationale: Glucose is broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water.

explanation: In aerobic respiration glucose reacts with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, and energy is released.
hints: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely.

stem: True or false: respiration and breathing are the same process.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is chemical reactions in cells that release energy.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Breathing is the movement of air; respiration is the release of energy from food in every living cell.

explanation: Breathing (ventilation) moves air into and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical breakdown of nutrients such as glucose inside cells to release energy. Plants and bacteria respire but do not breathe.
hints: Do plants breathe with lungs? Do they respire?

stem: Which process in the human body needs energy from respiration?

options.content: Active transport of glucose into the cells lining the small intestine
options.rationale: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy.

options.content: Diffusion of oxygen from the alveoli into the blood
options.rationale: Diffusion is passive; it needs no energy from respiration.

options.content: Osmosis of water into the blood from the colon
options.rationale: Osmosis is passive.

options.content: Photosynthesis in the skin
options.rationale: Humans do not photosynthesise.

explanation: Active transport uses energy from respiration to move substances against a concentration gradient. Diffusion and osmosis are passive and need no energy from respiration.
hints: Which process moves substances against a concentration gradient?

stem: Name the cell organelle in which most aerobic respiration takes place.

rejected.feedback: The nucleus contains the genetic material.

explanation: Most aerobic respiration takes place in the mitochondria, which is why very active cells such as muscle cells contain many of them.
hints: Muscle cells contain very many of these organelles.

stem: Complete the sentence about aerobic respiration.

payload.template: In aerobic respiration, glucose reacts with {{blank:ox}} to produce {{blank:co2}} and {{blank:h2o}}.

explanation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Energy is released, but it is not a substance.
hints: It is the reverse of the word equation for photosynthesis.

stem: (Supplement) Which is the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration?

options.rationale: This is the equation for photosynthesis.
This is not balanced: the numbers of atoms differ on the two sides.
Six of each: oxygen, carbon dioxide and water.
This is anaerobic respiration in yeast.

explanation: Aerobic respiration: $\ce{C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O}$. Each glucose molecule reacts with six oxygen molecules to give six carbon dioxide and six water molecules.
hints: Count the carbon atoms: glucose has six.

stem: (Supplement) How many molecules of carbon dioxide are produced when 5 molecules of glucose are respired aerobically?
explanation: Each glucose molecule produces 6 molecules of carbon dioxide ($\ce{C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O}$), so 5 glucose molecules produce $5 \times 6 = 30$.
workedSolution:
1. From the balanced equation, 1 glucose gives 6 $\ce{CO2}$.
2. $5 \times 6 = 30$ molecules of carbon dioxide.
hints: Use the numbers in the balanced equation.

stem: Match each use of energy from respiration with an example.

right.content: A cell making enzymes from amino acids
New skin cells forming to repair a cut
A dog staying at 38 °C on a cold night

explanation: The heart beats by muscle contraction; enzymes are made by protein synthesis; repairing a cut needs cell division; mammals release heat from respiration to stay warm. Diffusion needs no energy from respiration.
hints: One example is a passive process that needs no energy.

stem: Yeast in sugar solution gave off bubbles of carbon dioxide fastest at 40 °C. At 60 °C no bubbles were produced. What is the best explanation for the result at 60 °C?

options.content: All the sugar had been used up.
options.rationale: The same sugar solution was used at every temperature.

options.content: The enzymes that control respiration were denatured.
options.rationale: High temperature changes the shape of the enzymes' active sites.

options.content: Carbon dioxide does not form bubbles at 60 °C.
options.rationale: Gas forms bubbles at any of these temperatures.

options.content: Yeast only respires in the cold.
options.rationale: Yeast respired fastest at 40 °C.

explanation: Respiration is controlled by enzymes. At 60 °C their active sites change shape (they are denatured), so the reactions stop and no carbon dioxide is produced.
hints: Respiration is a series of enzyme-controlled reactions.

stem: In an experiment to show that germinating seeds release heat, the control flask contains seeds that have been boiled and then rinsed in disinfectant. Why are they rinsed in disinfectant?

options.content: To make the seeds germinate faster
options.rationale: The control seeds are dead and cannot germinate.

options.content: To add moisture to the flask
options.rationale: Disinfectant is used to kill microorganisms, not to add moisture.

options.content: To stop heat escaping from the flask
options.rationale: The vacuum flask stops heat escaping.

options.content: To kill microorganisms that would respire on the dead seeds and release heat
options.rationale: Then any temperature rise in the other flask must be due to the living seeds.

explanation: Bacteria and fungi would feed on the dead seeds and respire, releasing heat. Disinfectant kills them, so the control shows that without living seeds the temperature does not rise.
hints: Which other organisms could respire in the control flask?

stem: Maggots were placed on a gauze above hydrogencarbonate indicator in a sealed tube. After an hour the indicator had changed from red to yellow. What does this show?

options.content: The maggots used up carbon dioxide.
options.rationale: Using up carbon dioxide would turn the indicator purple.

options.content: The maggots produced oxygen.
options.rationale: Animals do not produce oxygen.

options.content: The maggots produced carbon dioxide by respiration.
options.rationale: More carbon dioxide turns the indicator yellow.

options.content: The indicator was heated by the maggots.
options.rationale: The colour change is caused by carbon dioxide, not heat.

explanation: Hydrogencarbonate indicator turns yellow when the carbon dioxide concentration rises. The maggots respired, producing carbon dioxide. A control tube with glass beads instead of maggots would stay red.
hints: Yellow means more carbon dioxide.

stem: Why is ATP described as the 'energy currency' of the cell?

options.content: Energy from respiration is used to make ATP, which is then broken down wherever energy is needed.
options.rationale: Like money, it is earned in one place and spent in another.

options.content: ATP is a store of glucose that the cell can respire later.
options.rationale: ATP is not glucose; it carries energy released from glucose.

options.content: ATP is made in photosynthesis only.
options.rationale: In animals ATP is made by respiration.

options.content: ATP is the enzyme that controls respiration.
options.rationale: ATP is not an enzyme.

explanation: Respiration releases energy that is used to make ATP from ADP and phosphate. ATP then moves to where energy is needed and is broken down to ADP and phosphate, releasing energy in small, usable amounts.
hints: Think of energy being 'earned' in respiration and 'spent' elsewhere.

stem: True or false: energy released in respiration is used to make ATP from ADP and phosphate.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. ATP is then broken down where energy is needed.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Respiration provides the energy to join ADP and phosphate, making ATP.

explanation: Energy released in respiration is used to join ADP and phosphate to make ATP. When ATP is broken down to ADP and phosphate, the energy is released for use in the cell.
hints: ATP has one more phosphate than ADP.

stem: Tatenda says that plants do not respire during the day because they are photosynthesising. Which statement is correct?

options.content: Tatenda is right: plants respire only at night.
options.rationale: Respiration never stops in living cells.

options.content: Plants respire all the time; in daylight photosynthesis is usually faster, so they give out more oxygen than they use.
options.rationale: Respiration continues day and night.

options.content: Plants never respire, because they make their own food.
options.rationale: Every living cell respires to release energy.

options.content: Plants respire only when there is no carbon dioxide.
options.rationale: Respiration does not depend on the absence of carbon dioxide.

explanation: All living cells respire all the time. During the day, photosynthesis in a well-lit plant is usually faster than respiration, so the plant takes in more carbon dioxide and gives out more oxygen than respiration alone would suggest.
hints: Do plant cells need energy at all times?

stem: A student counted 84 bubbles of gas released by a yeast culture in 4 minutes. Calculate the rate of bubble production per minute.
explanation: Rate $= \dfrac{84}{4} = 21$ bubbles per minute.
workedSolution: 1. Rate $= \dfrac{\text{number of bubbles}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{84}{4} = 21$ bubbles per minute.
hints: Divide the number of bubbles by the time.

stem:
Nyasha investigated the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast. She counted the bubbles of gas produced in 5 minutes by the same mass of yeast in the same volume of sugar solution at five temperatures, repeating each three times.

| Temperature / °C | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 15 | 12 | 14 | 13 | 13 |
| 25 | 30 | 27 | 30 | 29 |
| 35 | 52 | 49 | 55 | ? |
| 45 | 41 | 38 | 38 | 39 |
| 55 | 6 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean number of bubbles at 35 °C.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean rate at 35 °C in bubbles per minute.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which conclusion about the optimum temperature is best supported?

options.content: The optimum is exactly 35 °C.
options.rationale: Only a few temperatures were tested, so the optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 45 °C.

options.content: The optimum lies between 25 °C and 45 °C, probably near 35 °C.
options.rationale: 35 °C gave the highest rate of those tested.

options.content: The optimum is 55 °C, because the yeast had warmed up.
options.rationale: The rate at 55 °C was the lowest.

options.content: There is no optimum; the rate rises with temperature.
options.rationale: The rate fell above 35 °C.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the rate was much lower at 55 °C than at 35 °C.

points.description: The enzymes controlling respiration were denatured (at high temperature)
Their active sites changed shape so the substrate no longer fitted, so fewer reactions / less carbon dioxide

parts.explanation: At 55 °C the enzymes that control respiration were being denatured: their active sites changed shape, so the substrate no longer fitted and far less carbon dioxide was produced.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** variables that Nyasha kept constant, and suggest **one** further improvement to her method.

points.description: Mass of yeast / volume or concentration of sugar solution / time of counting (any two)
Improvement: collect the gas in a gas syringe (bubbles vary in size) / test more temperatures around 35 °C / leave tubes to reach the temperature first

parts.explanation: She kept the mass of yeast and the volume and concentration of sugar solution the same. Bubbles vary in size, so collecting the gas in a gas syringe would be more accurate; testing more temperatures between 25 °C and 45 °C would find the optimum more precisely.

explanation: Mean at 35 °C $= \dfrac{52 + 49 + 55}{3} = 52$; rate $= \dfrac{52}{5} = 10.4$ bubbles per minute. The rate rises to a peak near 35 °C and falls at higher temperatures as the respiratory enzymes are denatured.
hints: The mean of three trials is their sum divided by 3.
Respiration is controlled by enzymes.

stem:
Chipo set up two vacuum flasks. Flask A contained soaked, germinating peas. Flask B contained the same number of peas that had been boiled and then rinsed in disinfectant. Each flask had a thermometer and a cotton wool plug.

| Day | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature in flask A / °C | 20.0 | 21.5 | 23.0 | 24.0 | 24.5 |
| Temperature in flask B / °C | 20.0 | 20.0 | 20.0 | 20.5 | 20.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rise in temperature in flask A over the four days.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the temperature rose in flask A.

points.description: The germinating peas respire (aerobically)
Respiration releases some energy as heat, which the vacuum flask stops escaping

parts.explanation: The germinating peas were respiring. Respiration releases some of its energy as heat, and the vacuum flask stopped the heat escaping, so the temperature rose.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the purpose of flask B?

options.content: To provide extra heat for flask A
options.rationale: The flasks are separate.

options.content: To show that boiled peas respire faster
options.rationale: Boiled peas are dead and do not respire.

options.content: It is a control: it shows the temperature rise in A is caused by living peas
options.rationale: Everything is the same except that the peas are dead.

options.content: To measure the temperature of the room
options.rationale: A thermometer outside the flasks would do that.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why flask B rose to 20.5 °C on day 3.

points.description: A change in room temperature / measurement error / a few microorganisms surviving (anomalous or chance variation)

parts.explanation: A small change in room temperature, a reading error or a few surviving microorganisms could explain it; the value returned to 20.0 °C on day 4.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why cotton wool, rather than a rubber bung, was used to close the flasks.

points.description: Allows oxygen to enter (and carbon dioxide to leave) so the peas can continue to respire aerobically

parts.explanation: Cotton wool lets air through, so oxygen can reach the peas for aerobic respiration and carbon dioxide can escape.

explanation: Germinating peas respire and release heat, so flask A warmed by 4.5 °C; flask B, with dead, disinfected peas, stayed at about 20 °C, showing that living seeds caused the rise. Cotton wool lets oxygen in for aerobic respiration.
hints: What do living seeds do that dead ones cannot?
Why might the peas need air?

stem: Describe how the energy released by respiration is used in the human body. Give **five** different uses. [5]

points.description: Muscle contraction (movement, heartbeat, breathing)
Protein synthesis (making enzymes, antibodies, hormones)
Cell division (growth, repair)
Active transport (e.g. absorbing glucose in the small intestine, kidney reabsorption)
Growth
Passage of nerve impulses
Keeping a constant body temperature (heat release)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Energy from respiration is used for muscle contraction, so that we can move, breathe and keep the heart beating. It is used in protein synthesis to build enzymes, antibodies and hormones from amino acids, and in cell division for growth and for repairing damaged tissue. Active transport uses it to move substances against a concentration gradient, for example when the small intestine absorbs glucose. Nerve impulses need energy to pass along neurones. Some of the energy is released as heat, which keeps the body at a constant temperature of about 37 °C.

explanation: Uses include muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses and keeping body temperature constant.
hints: Give a specific process for each use, not just 'for energy'.

stem: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the rate of respiration of yeast. Include the variables you would control, how you would measure the rate, and how you would make your results reliable. [6]

points.description: Yeast suspended in sugar (glucose) solution in tubes / flasks
Placed in water baths at a range of temperatures, e.g. 10–60 °C (at least five values)
Leave to reach the temperature before starting timing
Measure rate: count bubbles per minute / gas volume in a syringe in a set time / time for limewater or indicator to change
Control: same mass / concentration of yeast
Control: same volume and concentration of sugar solution / same time
Repeat at each temperature and calculate a mean; identify anomalies
Control experiment with boiled yeast / no yeast

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Mix the same mass of yeast with the same volume of the same concentration of glucose solution in six boiling tubes. Stand each tube in a thermostatically controlled water bath at a different temperature, for example 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C, and leave them for five minutes to reach the temperature. Connect each tube to a gas syringe and record the volume of gas collected in 10 minutes (or count the bubbles per minute through a delivery tube); the faster the gas is produced, the faster the rate of respiration. Keep the yeast mass, the glucose volume and concentration and the timing the same. Set up a control tube with boiled yeast to show that living yeast produces the gas. Repeat the investigation three times at each temperature, calculate the mean and look for anomalous results.

explanation: A good plan names the independent variable (temperature) and its range, the dependent variable and how it is measured, the controlled variables, a control and repeats.
hints: What will you change, what will you measure, and what will you keep the same?

stem: A mouse uses much more energy per gram of body mass each day than a lizard of the same mass, even when both are resting. What is the most likely reason?

options.content: The mouse has more mitochondria in its skin.
options.rationale: This does not explain the large difference in energy use.

options.content: The lizard does not respire at all.
options.rationale: All living organisms respire.

options.content: The mouse photosynthesises less than the lizard.
options.rationale: Neither animal photosynthesises.

options.content: The mouse uses energy from respiration to keep its body temperature constant.
options.rationale: Mammals release heat from respiration to stay warm; lizards rely on the Sun.

explanation: Mammals such as mice keep a constant, high body temperature using heat released by respiration, so they respire much faster than reptiles, whose body temperature depends on their surroundings.
hints: Which of the two keeps a constant body temperature?

stem: A respirometer contained 10 germinating mung bean seeds on a gauze platform above soda lime, which absorbs carbon dioxide. A drop of coloured liquid in a narrow tube attached to the respirometer moved 18 mm towards the seeds in 10 minutes at 20 °C. A control respirometer, set up in the same way with glass beads instead of seeds, showed no movement.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of movement of the coloured liquid in mm per minute.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the coloured liquid moved towards the seeds.

points.description: The seeds took in oxygen for (aerobic) respiration
and the carbon dioxide they gave out was absorbed by the soda lime, so the volume (pressure) of gas fell and the liquid was drawn in

parts.explanation: The seeds used oxygen in aerobic respiration. The carbon dioxide they released was absorbed by the soda lime, so the volume of gas inside fell and the liquid was pulled towards the seeds.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the purpose of the control respirometer with glass beads.

points.description: To show that the movement is caused by the living seeds (not by changes in temperature or pressure)

parts.explanation: It shows that the movement is caused by the living, respiring seeds, not by changes in temperature or air pressure.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The experiment was repeated at 30 °C. What result is expected?

options.content: The liquid moves faster, because respiration is faster at 30 °C
options.rationale: Respiratory enzymes work faster at 30 °C than at 20 °C.

options.content: The liquid moves more slowly, because enzymes are denatured at 30 °C
options.rationale: 30 °C is below the temperature that denatures these enzymes.

options.content: The liquid does not move, because seeds do not respire at 30 °C
options.rationale: Seeds respire across a wide range of temperatures.

options.content: The liquid moves away from the seeds
options.rationale: The seeds still use oxygen, so the liquid moves towards them.

explanation: Rate $= \dfrac{18}{10} = 1.8$ mm per minute. Respiring seeds take in oxygen; the soda lime absorbs the carbon dioxide they release, so the gas volume falls and the liquid moves towards them. The glass-bead control shows the movement is due to living seeds. A warmer temperature (below the denaturing range) speeds up respiration.
hints: Which gas is used and which gas is absorbed?
What does the soda lime remove?
